extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy, history, and public administration
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted principles and evaluative statements about military organization, the cost of state functions, and the origins of social subordination from a political-economy treatise. Includes causes of authority, the role and cost of standing armies, and the administration of justice in societies at different stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing army superiority over militia
rubrics_metrics.description: A well regulated standing army is superior to every militia; it alone can defend an opulent and civilized nation against invasion and perpetuate civilization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Hannibal's standing army in Spain, the Roman standing armies after the second Punic war, and modern standing armies' advantage over militias. Anti-pattern: relying on militia exposes civilized nations to conquest by barbarous neighbours; victories by militias are generally over other, less disciplined militias rather than standing armies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of discipline through continuous service
rubrics_metrics.description: Armies continuously employed in the field become gradually formed to the exact discipline of a standing army, making them superior to militia raised ad hoc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Carthaginian armies under Amilcar, Asdrubal, and Hannibal; Roman militias became standing armies only after prolonged engagement. Scoring note: longevity and continuous engagement correlate with discipline and effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expense of defence grows with civilization
rubrics_metrics.description: The sovereign's duty of defending society becomes more expensive as society advances in civilization; military force which cost nothing originally must be maintained in peace and war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Expect increasing fiscal burdens on the state as population, property, and military technology advance. The growing expense explains the transition from private maintenance of defence to taxation-funded standing armies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of firearms on military cost and advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention of firearms has greatly increased the expense of exercising and disciplining soldiers and of fortifying towns; thus it advantages opulent and civilized nations over poor and barbarous ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and specifics: muskets, cannon, mortars are costlier and heavier than ancient arms; powder consumed in training is irrecoverable; modern artillery makes fortifications much more expensive. Anti-pattern: underestimating logistical and materiel costs when adopting firearm-based forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing armies as instruments of state-building and civilization
rubrics_metrics.description: A standing army can establish the sovereign's law and maintain regular government across remote provinces, thereby facilitating sudden and tolerable civilization of barbarous regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Peter the Great's reforms in Russia largely resolved into establishing a well regulated standing army which executed and maintained other regulations and order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil-military alignment determines danger to liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: A standing army is dangerous to liberty when the interests of its leaders are not connected with supporting the constitution; it is less dangerous (and may favor liberty) when the sovereign is general and principal officers are those with greatest stake in civil order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Caesar's standing army destroyed the Roman republic; Cromwell's army displaced Parliament. Counter-example: where officers are landed nobility whose interests align with civil authority, the army can stabilize rather than threaten liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quartering and dispersion degrade standing armies
rubrics_metrics.description: Withdrawing standing armies from frontiers and quartering small bodies in towns transforms soldiers into tradesmen and artificers, leading to degeneration of military discipline and a civil character that weakens defence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical claim: Diocletian or Constantine dispersed legions into provincial towns, causing standing armies to degenerate into neglected militias incapable of resisting invasions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Militia vulnerability to barbarous nations
rubrics_metrics.description: Civilized nations that depend on militia are at continual risk of conquest by nearby barbarous nations whose militias (e.g., shepherd-warrior types) are naturally superior in certain contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: frequent conquests of Asian civilizations by Tartars; superiority of Scythian/Tartar militias over some civilized forces. Implication: militia alone is insufficient for long-term defence of civilized polities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property necessitates civil government and judicial expense
rubrics_metrics.description: The acquisition of valuable and extensive property makes civil government and an administration of justice necessary because property owners need protection from invasion and injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: In societies with little property (hunters) formal magistracy is less necessary; as property grows, so do demands for judicial institutions and their associated expenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four natural causes of subordination and authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Subordination and social rank naturally arise from four causes: (1) superiority of personal qualifications (strength, wisdom, virtue), (2) superiority of age, (3) superiority of fortune, and (4) superiority of birth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each cause is explained with examples: age as plain, palpable quality; fortune most powerful in rudest societies; birth follows fortune and implies antiquity of family wealth. Use these axes to analyze origins of social hierarchy in different societal stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of fortune and birth in establishing authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Superiority of fortune and antiquity of family (birth) are principal sources of personal distinction and thus establish authority and subordination, especially among societies of shepherds and early husbandmen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Tartar chiefs using flocks to maintain followers; ancient families retaining reverence and authority. Anti-pattern: assuming personal merit alone suffices to establish permanent authority in unequal societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administration of justice as revenue source and corruption risk
rubrics_metrics.description: When judicial office fees, presents, and amercements constitute ordinary sovereign revenue, the administration of justice becomes a source of revenue and thus tends toward corruption, delay, and partiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: judges of Henry II's circuit acted as itinerant factors levying revenue; presents bias outcomes; amercements incentivised wrongful verdicts. Remedial move: regulation/abolition of fees when the sovereign's revenue is sourced by taxation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition from fee-based justice to tax-funded abolition of presents
rubrics_metrics.description: As defence costs compel taxation and the sovereign's private estate becomes insufficient, societies commonly stipulate that no presents for justice be accepted, abolishing fees considered impossible to regulate fairly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Policy implication—shifting funding of justice away from ad hoc presents reduces corruption; historical explanation for reforms abolishing judicial fees when state revenue is centralized through taxes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial delegation trades impartiality for revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: Delegating judicial authority to bailiffs/judges who must account to principals for profits leads to abuses, especially when those officials act to please superiors or extract revenue, making redress difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in barbarous governments and post-Roman Europe, delegated judges exercised jurisdiction to garner revenue for sovereign or themselves; redress was often impossible when abuses served sovereign interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military capacity influences imperial ambition and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature and limits of an empire's conquests are shaped by the relative strength and composition of its military (standing armies vs militias) and judgments about whether further conquest is worth the cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Romans did not pursue final conquest of Parthia or Germany possibly because it was not worth adding barbarous countries to an already large empire. Practical note: military logistics and costs constrain expansionist policy.
